turns.user:
I'm a Product Manager (IC6) at Meta in the Bay Area. Google reached out to me. I wasn't looking and I'm happy where I am, but after interviewing they've made me an offer for a Senior Product Manager role (L6) in San Francisco.

At Meta I make $240,000 base, a bonus of about $36,000, and about $250,000/yr in vesting RSUs, so roughly $526,000/yr. About $200,000 of RSUs would vest in my next 12 months if I stayed.

The offer:
- Base salary: $235,000
- Target annual bonus: 20% of base ($47,000)
- New-hire RSUs: $1,080,000, vesting over 4 years
- No sign-on bonus

The job posting listed a base salary range of $183,000 to $271,000.

What the recruiter told me:
- Google gives annual equity refresh grants that stack over time, since each one vests over several years. The recruiter was clear that refreshes aren't guaranteed.

Compensation matters a lot to me. Is this a good offer? Should I accept it, negotiate, or walk away? If I negotiate, what exactly should I ask for, and how much?
turns.reply:
## Bottom line

**Negotiate. Don’t accept the first offer, but don’t walk away yet.**

The offer is **market-competitive but not compelling enough for someone who is happy at Meta and prioritizes compensation**. Its four-year annualized value is almost exactly the current Bay Area median reported for Google L6 PMs—roughly $551,500—so this looks more like a standard offer than a premium “convince me to leave Meta” package. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

I would ask for:

- **Base:** $265,000  
- **New-hire equity:** $1,400,000  
- **Sign-on:** $150,000–$200,000  

A good settlement would be approximately:

- **Base:** $250,000–$260,000
- **Equity:** $1,250,000–$1,350,000
- **Sign-on:** $75,000–$150,000

If Google leaves the offer essentially unchanged, I would probably stay at Meta unless the role is substantially better for your career or quality of life.

---

## How the current offer actually compares

### Four-year annualized comparison

|  | Meta normalized | Google offer |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240,000 | $235,000 |
| Target/typical bonus | $36,000 | $47,000 |
| Annualized equity | $250,000 | $270,000 |
| **Annualized TC** | **$526,000** | **$552,000** |

So the Google offer provides only:

- **$26,000 more annually**
- Approximately a **5% premium**
- Lower base salary
- More target bonus risk
- Dependence on uncertain future refresh grants

For a voluntary move from a job you like, **5% is not enough of a risk premium** in my view.

Your actual next 12 months at Meta are somewhat lower:

- $240,000 base
- $36,000 bonus
- $200,000 scheduled RSUs
- **$476,000 forward 12-month TC**

But you shouldn’t evaluate the move only against that temporary trough. Your stated normalized Meta compensation is $526,000, and you may receive future Meta refreshes if you stay.

---

## The vesting schedule matters enormously

Google’s new-hire grants are commonly reported as front-loaded, currently around **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%**, although you must get your specific schedule confirmed in writing. Alphabet’s public filings confirm RSUs generally vest over four years, but do not establish your exact percentages. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000165204426000018/goog-20251231.htm?utm_source=openai))

If your $1.08 million grant follows 38/32/20/10, and ignoring stock-price changes and refreshes:

| Year | Base + target bonus | New-hire RSUs | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $282,000 | $410,400 | **$692,400** |
| 2 | $282,000 | $345,600 | **$627,600** |
| 3 | $282,000 | $216,000 | **$498,000** |
| 4 | $282,000 | $108,000 | **$390,000** |

This tells two different stories:

1. **Years 1–2 look excellent.** The first-year Google equity would more than replace the $200,000 vesting at Meta.
2. **Years 3–4 are weak without meaningful refreshes.** By year four, you would be $136,000 below your current normalized Meta compensation, before accounting for Meta refreshes or raises.

Google does have a structured annual process that includes modeled equity refresh recommendations based on factors such as performance, role, and location, followed by management review. But that does not make any particular refresher guaranteed. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Therefore, **do not let the recruiter sell this primarily using first-year TC**. Evaluate:

- Four-year average
- Year-four cliff
- When you become eligible for your first refresh
- How refreshes vest
- What a normal “meets expectations” L6 PM refresh looks like

---

## What I would negotiate

### Opening request

Ask for all three components:

> I’m very excited about the team and role. At the same time, I wasn’t actively looking and I’m happy at Meta, so the compensation needs to make the transition clearly compelling. My current normalized compensation is approximately $526,000, and I have about $200,000 of equity vesting over the next 12 months.
>
> On a four-year annualized basis, the current Google offer is about $552,000, which is only a modest premium over staying, particularly given the uncertainty around future refresh grants and the back-end decline in the initial grant.
>
> To make the move work, I’d like to explore a package around a **$265,000 base, $1.4 million new-hire equity grant, and a $200,000 sign-on bonus** to offset the equity I’m leaving behind. I’m flexible on how the package is allocated if there are constraints on any one component.

That is an assertive but defensible anchor:

- $265,000 is within the posted $183,000–$271,000 base range.
- Your current base is already $240,000.
- You have a strong BATNA: remaining happily employed at Meta.
- There is no sign-on in the initial package.
- The offer is approximately market median, rather than unusually strong.

### Why $1.4 million equity?

At $260,000 base, 20% bonus and $1.4 million equity:

- Base: $260,000
- Bonus: $52,000
- Annualized equity: $350,000
- **Annualized TC: $662,000**

That is approximately a 26% premium over your current $526,000. You may not get all of it, but it is a reasonable “make me leave” anchor.

### Your likely settlement target

A realistic strong outcome might be:

- $255,000 base
- $1.3 million equity
- $100,000 sign-on

That package produces:

- $255,000 base
- $51,000 target bonus
- $325,000 annualized equity
- **$631,000 recurring annualized TC**
- Plus $100,000 one-time cash

That is meaningfully better than Meta rather than merely nominally better.

---

## How to prioritize the components

My order would be:

1. **Base**
2. **Equity**
3. **Sign-on**

Base is especially valuable because every additional dollar also increases the 20% target bonus. Raising base from $235,000 to $260,000 adds:

- $25,000 in salary
- $5,000 in target bonus
- **$30,000 per year**, or approximately $120,000 over four years before raises

Equity is probably the easiest way for Google to make a major adjustment. Sign-on is useful for compensating forfeited Meta equity and transition risk, but it is nonrecurring.

If they say the sign-on is constrained, respond:

> If a cash sign-on isn’t available, I’d be open to shifting that value into the initial equity grant. My main objective is to get the overall four-year package to a level that makes leaving my current position compelling.

If they say base is constrained:

> I understand. In that case, could we solve for the gap through additional new-hire equity and a sign-on payment?

Do not immediately volunteer your minimum.

---

## What to clarify before deciding

Ask the recruiter for written answers to these:

1. **What is the exact new-hire vesting schedule?**  
   Is it 38/32/20/10, 33/33/22/12, or something else?

2. **What are the first vest date and vesting frequency?**  
   Also ask when the number of shares is determined. Alphabet says the grant date for new hires is typically the first non-holiday Wednesday of the month after the employee starts, which can create stock-price exposure between accepting and the grant date. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000130817925000511/goog_courtesy-pdf.pdf?utm_source=openai))

3. **When would you first be eligible for an equity refresh?**  
   If you join in late 2026 or early 2027, are you eligible in the next compensation cycle, partially eligible, or excluded?

4. **How do refresh grants vest?**  
   Do they vest evenly over four years, and when does the first portion vest?

5. **What is the modeled or typical refresh for an L6 PM with a solid performance rating?**  
   They may refuse to provide a number, but ask anyway. Phrase it as a range or representative example rather than a promise.

6. **Is the bonus prorated during the first year?**

7. **Does the offer include any guaranteed first-year bonus or compensation protection?**

8. **Can the sign-on be structured in two installments?**  
   For example, $100,000 at joining and $50,000 after one year, if that is easier to approve.

---

## My decision thresholds

### I would be inclined to accept

If the final offer reaches approximately:

- **$250,000–$260,000 base**
- **$1.25–$1.35 million equity**
- **At least $75,000–$100,000 sign-on**

That creates a meaningful premium and reduces the risk of leaving a job you already like.

### I would consider accepting, but only for a particularly attractive role

Something around:

- $250,000 base
- $1.2 million equity
- $50,000–$100,000 sign-on

That is approximately $600,000 of recurring annualized TC, plus sign-on—roughly a 14% premium over your normalized Meta compensation.

### I would probably stay at Meta

If Google remains near:

- $235,000 base
- $1.08 million equity
- No sign-on

That offer is fair in the abstract, but **not sufficiently compelling for your specific situation**. You would be taking organizational, manager, scope and performance-calibration risk for only about a 5% normalized premium, with a substantial year-three/year-four compensation cliff unless refreshes materialize.

**Recommendation: negotiate aggressively but professionally, target roughly $650,000 annualized TC, and require at least about $600,000–$625,000 plus some sign-on before moving solely for compensation.**

turns.user: Update: I told the recruiter I'd be walking away from about $200,000 of RSUs that would vest in the next 12 months. Final offer: base $240,000, RSUs raised to $1,280,000 (vesting over 4 years), and no sign-on bonus. They said this is their best offer. Should I take it?
turns.reply:
## My recommendation: **lean yes—take it**, assuming you like the manager, scope, and team

The revised offer is materially better. It has crossed from “fair but not compelling” to **financially compelling enough to justify leaving**, although it still isn’t an obvious choice if you strongly prefer your current Meta role.

I would **stop negotiating** after they have explicitly called this their best offer. Instead, confirm the vesting details and make the decision.

## The economics

### Annualized four-year value

|  | Meta current run rate | Google offer |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240,000 | $240,000 |
| Bonus | ~$36,000 | $48,000 target |
| Annualized initial equity | ~$250,000 | $320,000 |
| **Annualized TC** | **$526,000** | **$608,000** |

That is:

- **$82,000 more per year**
- A **15.6% increase**
- **$328,000 more over four years**, ignoring raises, stock movement, and refresh grants at either company

Your Google offer also appears strong relative to recent self-reported L6 PM compensation. One October 2026 analysis of Levels.fyi data put US Google L6 PM median TC around $514,000 and the 90th percentile around $671,000. Your $608,000 annualized package is therefore well above the reported median, though not at the very top of the range. ([aakashg.com](https://www.aakashg.com/google-pm-job-offer/?utm_source=openai))

## The $200,000 you’re “walking away from”

Economically, Google has now addressed most of this concern—even without a cash sign-on.

They increased the grant from $1.08 million to $1.28 million, exactly **$200,000 in additional grant value**. It isn’t equivalent to $200,000 cash today because:

- You must remain employed for it to vest.
- Its value depends on Alphabet’s share price.
- The additional equity vests over time rather than immediately.

But you aren’t simply forfeiting $200,000 and getting nothing in return. You’re exchanging the Meta vest for a substantially larger Google vesting stream.

Your forward 12-month Meta compensation is approximately:

- $240,000 base
- $36,000 bonus
- $200,000 RSUs
- **$476,000 total**

Even if Google’s grant vested evenly at 25% annually, first-year target compensation would be:

- $240,000 base
- $48,000 target bonus
- $320,000 equity
- **$608,000 total**

That is **$132,000 above your next 12 months at Meta**.

## Confirm the exact vesting schedule

Alphabet’s filings confirm that RSUs generally vest over four years, but you need your specific schedule in writing. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000165204426000018/goog-20251231.htm?utm_source=openai))

If your grant uses Google’s commonly reported front-loaded **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%** schedule, the picture would be:

| Year | Equity vesting | Google target TC | Difference vs $526K Meta run rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $486,400 | **$774,400** | +$248,400 |
| 2 | $409,600 | **$697,600** | +$171,600 |
| 3 | $256,000 | **$544,000** | +$18,000 |
| 4 | $128,000 | **$416,000** | –$110,000 |

The front-loaded schedule remains commonly reported for Google new-hire grants, but schedules can vary, so do not sign based on this assumption alone. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule?utm_source=openai))

If that is your schedule, Google would pay approximately **$470,000 more than Meta over the first two years**, comparing Google’s $1.472 million with one year of your $476,000 forward Meta compensation and one year at your $526,000 run rate.

That makes the absence of a sign-on much less concerning. The real concern becomes the **year-three/year-four cliff**, not the first-year transition.

## What could make staying at Meta better?

I would stay at Meta instead if several of these are true:

- You materially prefer your current manager, team, or product.
- Your current role has stronger promotion prospects.
- You expect a substantial Meta refresh grant soon.
- Your $250,000 annual Meta equity run rate is likely to continue or increase.
- The Google role has unclear scope, an unattractive manager, or reorganization risk.
- You expect to remain at Google for four-plus years but have little confidence in refresh grants.

The $328,000 four-year headline advantage is real, but it is not guaranteed economic profit. Changing companies introduces performance-calibration, team, reorganization, promotion, and employment-duration risk.

Also, a significant Meta refresh could erase the difference. For example, additional Meta compensation averaging roughly **$82,000 per year above your present assumptions** would bring the four-year packages close to parity.

## The refresh question

Do not count any Google refresh in your decision model because the recruiter has correctly said it is not guaranteed. Treat it as upside.

But before signing, ask for written confirmation of:

1. The precise percentage vesting in each of the four years.
2. Vesting frequency and first vest date.
3. When the grant is converted from dollars into shares.
4. Whether you will be eligible for the next annual refresh cycle.
5. Whether first-year bonus eligibility is prorated.
6. Whether there are any delayed-vesting or grant-date complications based on your start date.

New-hire Alphabet grants are typically dated on the first non-holiday Wednesday of the month after the employee starts, meaning the share count may not be fixed on the date you accept. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000130817925000511/goog_courtesy-pdf.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## Final decision rule

I would frame it this way:

- **Role/team at Google at least as attractive as Meta:** Take Google.
- **Google role somewhat less attractive, but tolerable:** Probably still take it if compensation is your leading priority, particularly with front-loaded vesting.
- **You substantially prefer Meta and value stability:** Stay. A 15.6% annualized premium is meaningful, but not enough to accept a role you expect to like significantly less.
- **You expect a near-term Meta promotion or major refresh:** Pause and include that in the comparison before signing.

### My call based on what you’ve said

Because compensation matters a lot, Google added $200,000 in equity, your base is now protected, and the package is approximately **$608,000 annualized**, I would **accept—provided the role and manager clear a basic quality bar and the vesting schedule is confirmed**.

I would not reject this solely because there is no sign-on. The equity increase makes the total package strong enough, and with front-loaded vesting, your first two years are particularly attractive. The sensible strategy would be to join, evaluate the role and refresh trajectory after 18–24 months, and avoid assuming that you must remain through the year-four cliff.
